citations.quote: Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

Assume countable choice. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the wavelet or trigonometric basis from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. Let $Z_{lk}$ be mutually independent real random variables with density $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Define the formal white-noise coefficient sequence $W=(Z_{lk})$. For every $\delta>1/2$, this sequence is almost surely an element of $H(\delta)$ and is a Borel Gaussian random element there. Its law $N$ is a Borel probability on $H(\delta)$. For an infinite-dimensional basis, white noise is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued random element. Here Gaussian means that each continuous real linear functional has a centered law $N(0,v)$ in the density convention of [[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series]]; in particular, for $L(c)=\sum_jd_jc_j$ its variance is $\sum_jd_j^2$ whenever this pairing is continuous on $H(\delta)$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $N$ let $V_N=\operatorname{span}\{u_1,\ldots,u_N\}$ and let $P_Ng=\sum_{j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$. Orthonormality gives $g-P_Ng\perp V_N$. For any $v\in H$, expanding the inner product of $v=P_Nv+(v-P_Nv)$ gives $\|v\|^2=\|P_Nv\|^2+\|v-P_Nv\|^2$, so $\|P_Nv\|\le\|v\|$. Given $\eta>0$, density of the finite span in [F2] gives $w\in V_M$ with $\|g-w\|<\eta$; for $N\ge M$, $P_Nw=w$, so $\|g-P_Ng\|\le\|g-w\|+\|P_N(w-g)\|\le2\|g-w\|<2\eta$. Thus $P_Ng\to g$ in norm, with the finite-basis case eventually equal to $g$.

For distinct indices $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, [F1] gives independent standard-normal variables $Z(u_{j_1}),\ldots,Z(u_{j_m})$. Since $\epsilon>0$, the affine map $z\mapsto\mu_{j_r}+\epsilon z$ and its inverse are continuous, so $Y_x(u_{j_r})$ and its noise coordinate generate the same sigma-algebra; independence therefore transfers. The affine-image definition of $N$ gives each law $N(\mu_{j_r},\epsilon^2)$.

Put $c_j=\langle g,u_j\rangle_H$. The linearity clause in [F1] applied to the finite sum defining $P_Ng$ gives $Z(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\le N}c_jZ(u_j)$; linearity of the inner product gives $\langle Kx,P_Ng\rangle_H=\sum_{j\le N}c_j\mu_j$. Combining these identities yields $Y_x(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\le N}c_jY_x(u_j)$.

In the carrier case covered by [F4]–[F5], [F1] supplies independent coordinates with the common standard-normal density and [A1] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F5]. Hence [F5] makes the noise coefficient sequence a Borel Gaussian random element of $H(\delta)$; [F4] puts each deterministic signal $Kx$ in the same space. Their sum $Kx+\epsilon W$ is therefore an $H(\delta)$-valued Borel random element, and every continuous linear functional of it is a translate and positive rescaling of the corresponding centered Gaussian functional.

With $r_N=g-P_Ng$, linearity gives $Y_x(g)-Y_x(P_Ng)=\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(r_N)$. Centering and the covariance identity in [F1] give $\mathbb E Z(r_N)=0$ and $\mathbb E[Z(r_N)^2]=\|r_N\|_H^2$; expanding the square therefore shows that the squared mean-square error is $|\langle Kx,r_N\rangle_H|^2+\epsilon^2\|r_N\|_H^2$. By [F3] and step 1.1, both terms tend to zero, proving the asserted mean-square reconstruction. For any finite list of test vectors, the sum of their finitely many squared errors also tends to zero, so the coordinate reconstructions converge jointly in product mean square.

In the infinite-dimensional function-space case, if $Kx+\epsilon W$ were an $H$-valued sample on an event of probability one, then $W=((Kx+\epsilon W)-Kx)/\epsilon$ would also be $H$-valued there, since $Kx\in H$ and $\epsilon>0$. This contradicts [F5], so the sample is not $H$-valued.

derivations.claim: Since $e_1,e_2$ are orthonormal, [F1] gives independent standard-normal noises $Z(e_1),Z(e_2)$. Each observation is an invertible affine function of its noise coordinate because $\epsilon>0$, so it has the same generated sigma-algebra; the affine-image definition of $N$ gives the two asserted laws and preserves independence.

Linearity of the process gives $Y_x(g)=aY_x(e_1)+bY_x(e_2)$ as an equality of its almost-sure equivalence classes. The mean is $am_1+bm_2$, and the covariance identity in [F1] gives variance $\epsilon^2\|ae_1+be_2\|^2=\epsilon^2(a^2+b^2)$. If $a=b=0$, then $g=0$ and linearity gives $Y_x(0)=0$.

citations.quote: Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, where separable means having a countable dense subset, and let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space. A real isonormal Gaussian process on $H$ is a family $Z(g)$ of real random variables with finite second moments, indexed by $g\in H$, such that $g\mapsto[Z(g)]$ is linear into $L^2(\mathbb P)$, $\mathbb E Z(g)=0$, and $\mathbb E[Z(g)Z(h)]=\langle g,h\rangle_H$. It is also required that for every finite orthonormal tuple $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ the variables $Z(e_1),\ldots,Z(e_m)$ are independent and each has density $\varphi(t)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-t^2/2}$. For any finite list of vectors, expressing them in an orthonormal basis of their finite-dimensional span shows that their process values have the corresponding linear-image Gaussian law. Here $L^2(\mathbb P)$ identifies square-integrable random variables that agree almost surely. When $H\ne\{0\}$, all unit-vector marginals have the same law; write $N(a,\sigma^2)$ for the law of $a+\sigma Z(e)$ for any unit vector $e\in H$ and $\sigma\ge0$.

Let $H$ be a separable real Hilbert space with a fixed complete orthonormal basis $(u_j)$, indexed by either a finite initial segment of $\mathbb N$ or all of $\mathbb N$. Let $Y_x(g)=\langle Kx,g\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(g)$ be the isonormal white-noise experiment with $\epsilon>0$, and write $\mu_j=\langle Kx,u_j\rangle_H$. For every parameter $x$ and every basis index $j$, the observations $Y_x(u_j)$ are independent and have laws $N(\mu_j,\epsilon^2)$, where $N$ is the scalar normal law defined in the experiment.

For $g\in H$, set $P_Ng=\sum_{j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_Hu_j$, with $P_N=I$ once all vectors of a finite basis have been included. Then

$$Y_x(g)=L^2(\mathbb P)\text{-}\lim_{N\to\infty}\sum_{j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_HY_x(u_j).$$

Thus every finite collection of observation functionals is reconstructed from the coefficient sequence in mean square; this does not assert samplewise convergence or an $H$-valued observation. If $H=L^2([0,1])$ and the basis is one of the wavelet or trigonometric bases used to define the negative Sobolev carrier $H(\delta)$, then under countable choice and for $\delta>1/2$ the same coordinate sequence is a Borel Gaussian random element in $H(\delta)$ with mean coefficients $Kx$ and noise level $\epsilon$. In infinite dimension it is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued sample.

derivations.claim: Since $g=P_Ng+r_N$ and the process is linear by [F1], $Y_x(g)=Y_x(P_Ng)+Y_x(r_N)$. Applying [F2] to $P_Ng$, whose later finite projections equal $P_Ng$, gives $Y_x(P_Ng)=\sum_{j\le N}\langle g,u_j\rangle_HY_x(u_j)$; the definition gives $Y_x(r_N)=\langle h,r_N\rangle_H+\epsilon Z(r_N)$. This proves the displayed decomposition.

The residual $r_N$ is orthogonal to $u_1,\ldots,u_N$. If $r_N\ne0$, adjoining $r_N/\|r_N\|_H$ to these vectors gives a finite orthonormal tuple, so [F1] makes $Z(r_N/\|r_N\|_H)$ independent of the first $N$ coordinate noises; linearity gives $Z(r_N)=\|r_N\|_H Z(r_N/\|r_N\|_H)$ as an equality of its almost-sure equivalence classes. Since $\epsilon>0$, this noise and the tail observation are invertible affine functions of one another, so the tail observation is independent of the first $N$ coordinates. The covariance identity gives its variance $\epsilon^2\|r_N\|_H^2$ and its mean is $\langle h,r_N\rangle_H$. If $r_N=0$, both are zero.
